summary: A 1971 note by R. T. Braden on CCN as a Network Service Center, about the Computer Center at UCLA offering services to the network.

plainLanguage.summary: A note describing how a computing center could offer its services to everyone on the network.

subtitle: The UCLA Computing Center's hardware and services available to ARPANET users

tldr.problem: As the ARPANET grew, other sites needed to know what computing resources were available and how to use remote systems like UCLA's.
tldr.mechanism: R. T. Braden at UCLA documented the CCN's hardware (an IBM 360/91 with 4 million bytes of fast memory), software (FORTRAN, PL/1, assembler, and many other compilers), and services (remote job submission, interactive systems like URSA and APL, batch processing, and disk storage).
tldr.outcome: This RFC served as an early service advertisement, describing how RAND and other sites could remotely access UCLA's computing power for batch jobs, interactive sessions, and data storage.

today: RFC 90 is a historical snapshot of how shared computing resources were offered in the early ARPANET. It describes a batch-oriented, time-shared mainframe accessed remotely—a model that evolved into cloud computing. The service-oriented approach Braden described (advertising capabilities, charging for resources, supporting multiple access methods) is a direct ancestor of modern cloud platforms like AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure.

sections.title: CCN: A Service Center
sections.content: In January 1971, R. T. Braden described the Campus Computing Network (CCN) at UCLA as it prepared to connect to the ARPANET. CCN operated an IBM 360/91 with 4 million bytes of fast memory, capable of 2-6 million instructions per second. The goal was to offer this expensive computing resource to other ARPANET sites. The RFC documented the hardware, operating system (OS/360 MVT), available software, and planned services, addressing the needs of RAND and other interested sites.
sections.plainLanguage: UCLA had a powerful IBM computer and wanted to let other universities use it over the network. They described it so people would know what it could do.

sections.title: Software and Services
sections.content: CCN offered extensive software: FORTRAN, PL/1, Algol, Assembler, COBOL, LISP, and many others. Interactive systems included URSA (a batch submission system for display consoles), APL, OLMS, and IBM's TSO time-sharing system. The Remote Job Service (RJS) allowed remote batch terminals to submit OS/360 jobs and receive output. A QUICKRUN subsystem provided fast turnaround for simple jobs. Storage included 220 million bytes of online disk for source programs, 170 million for object modules, and 100 million bytes of temporary storage.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer had lots of programming languages, could handle jobs submitted from afar, and had lots of disk space. You could submit a job and get results back remotely.

sections.title: Cost-Competitive Processing
sections.content: CCN charged based on CPU time (T), input/output operations (I), and core memory size (R). The 360/91 was particularly cost-effective for compute-bound, heavy floating-point calculations, particularly those requiring large memory regions. The RFC noted that for most other types of jobs, CCN was competitive with other cost-recovery computing centers. Remote batch entry terminals communicated at rates from 2000 baud (dial-up) to 50,000 baud (dedicated lines).
sections.plainLanguage: Running a job cost money based on how much CPU time, disk, and memory it used. For math-heavy programs, it was a good deal compared to other supercomputers.
